messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajan is a 75-year-old South Asian man who came to the United States as a refugee decades ago, carrying with him a history that had never fully resolved into the past. He is married, soft-spoken, and has spent the better part of his adult life in America as a potter — a craft he brought from his homeland, one that once gave his days both structure and meaning. He presented for treatment with a PCL-5 score of 50, describing a constellation of symptoms that had worsened quietly over recent years until they could no longer be managed in silence.

The events that fractured Rajan's sense of safety occurred during the violence and forced displacement of his early life. He witnessed the deaths of people he loved — bodies carried past him, makeshift burials in disturbed earth, the sounds of vehicles and shouting that preceded raids on his village. Police and soldiers moved through his community with authority that meant terror rather than protection. The chaos was not a single event but an accumulated season of loss, and much of what Rajan experienced during that time has never organized itself into a coherent narrative. He reports that his memories of the period come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together — sensory fragments, images without context, a feeling of cold ground beneath his feet that arrives without any story attached. What he experienced was so overwhelming that he cannot seem to put it into words even now, though the memories themselves feel more real and vivid than anything from his ordinary life since.

It is precisely this quality of his memory — raw, wordless, and fragmented — that keeps the past so close to the surface. When a memory intrudes, it does not arrive as a recollection but as a reliving, and in its wake Rajan finds himself scanning his surroundings compulsively, reading every doorway and parking lot for signs of threat. This hypervigilant checking, which has become a near-constant feature of his daily life, reinforces his deepest fear: that he is no longer capable of being safe, that the world remains fundamentally dangerous, and that he lacks the inner resources to cope with even minor disturbances. His belief that he must be especially careful because you never know what can happen next is not an abstract worry but a felt certainty, one the fragmentary memories keep renewing.

These negative appraisals, in turn, make the memories harder to bear and easier to trigger. When Rajan believes he is incapable and perpetually at risk, any sensory echo of the original violence lands with amplified force. A car engine revving in the street outside his pottery studio is enough — the sound pulls him back before he can orient himself, his hands going still over the clay. Police cars, even parked ones he passes on his walk from the parking lot, send a current of alarm through him that takes hours to subside. Funerals are perhaps the most destabilizing: a neighbor's bereavement gathering last spring, with its gathering of dark-clothed figures and its proximity to a cemetery, left him unable to work for several days. The triggers, fed by the appraisals that have settled into his thinking like sediment, arrive with a frequency that exhausts him.

Over the years, Rajan has organized his life around avoidance in ways that have quietly narrowed it. He steers away from any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, which has meant withdrawing from community organizations he once valued. More painfully, he has begun avoiding situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful — celebrations, his grandchildren's recitals — because he has come to believe that positive feeling is a kind of exposure, a lowering of the guard that something terrible will punish. These avoidances have not brought relief; instead, they have deepened his conviction that he is fragile and diminished, that the man who once shaped vessels with steady hands is gone. The avoidance itself becomes a trigger for new intrusions, each retreat confirming that the world outside is as dangerous as he fears.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a conversation with his wife, who told him gently that she was losing him — not to death, but to disappearance. He arrived at intake hoping, tentatively, that some part of what he had been might still be recoverable. What he fears most is that it cannot be.
